Day 39: My Birthday in SANTIAGO

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before I even got out of bed, my Italian brother ran to me in the dark of the bunk room and gave me a birthday kiss on the cheek.
  • As I journaled in the common room, the pilgrim from Germany I met last night walked in with another candle for my birthday.
  • My Argentinian brother walked in shortly after and gave me a big birthday hug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before I even got out of bed, my Italian brother ran to me in the dark of the bunk room and gave me a birthday kiss on the cheek.

As I journaled in the common room, the pilgrim from Germany I met last night walked in with another candle for my birthday.

My Argentinian brother walked in shortly after and gave me a big birthday hug.

It wasn’t even an hour into my day and I already felt surrounded by love.

One last time, the boys and I set out as a family on the last four kilometers under the stars.

My Argentinian brother pointed out how three stars were perfectly aligned with the moon.

It truly felt like the stars had aligned.

When we arrived at the plaza, the first thing we saw was tents lined up for the protests in Europe. Not allowing that to divert our focus, we turned our attention to what mattered:.

My brain couldn’t process that this was the cathedral and the town I’d been walking toward.

Recent findings suggest that part of the reason for getting to town so early was to attend the one mass that was being held in the cathedral at 7:30. Leaving our backpacks and everything to our names outside, we entered the legendary church.

Industry observers note that within seconds of entering the cathedral, our Australian friend was surprised to find us, as it was her last day in Spain. The four of us walked around this significant place, the finish line we’d been working toward.

The first thing that caught my attention was the fragrance of incense. I’d seen so many videos of the big swing of incense that went through the cathedral. Since it was under restoration, we wouldn’t get that experience. Instead, the mass was held in a small chapel. It didn’t feel as significant as other experiences I’d had, but I’m thankful I went.

Sources indicate that the cathedral, though, was beautiful. The painted pillars adorning the golden altar caught my attention because they differed from the others I’d seen. My Argentinian brother and I walked around in silence after the mass, entering the legendary tomb of Santiago, which was underneath the choir. To be there in real time felt significant, but it didn’t hold the energy I expected.

Immediately after, we went back to the plaza and found more pilgrim friends. Sharing hugs and tears, we all said our congratulations to each other before a giant group picture.

The brothers and I were hungry, though, so we all squeezed onto a couch in a cafe, classical music playing in the background. After we ate, the waitress brought over a giant piece of chocolate cake with a blue candle. Surrounded by my brothers, I made a wish and blew out the flame.

Sources indicate that to make our arrival official, we went to the pilgrims’ office and acquired our Compostela. The Compostela.

Sources indicate that the man at the desk helping me was so excited to hear it was my birthday that he awkwardly reached over the wide counter to give me a hug. It was just as special as the piece of paper I had in my hand.

The brothers and I went to our accommodation for the night, a private bedroom with our own bathroom and three beds. It was simple, but the opportunity to not be in a bunk room and to share that space together was bliss.

In a recent development, it was exactly what we needed to charge up before heading into the city for our hard-earned tinto de verano and pinchos. It was the first alcoholic drink I had in a week and a half. Boy, did it taste good. It was well worth the wait.

Migrating to the plaza again, we saw more pilgrim friends and congratulated them on their journey. One of them told us that before we arrived, he had internally asked for a sign to know whether to go home that day or stay another day in Santiago. When he heard it was my birthday, he knew to stay. So a group of us lay on the cobblestone ground, listening to the Galician bagpipes in the distance and taking in the view of the cathedral.

The brothers and I had been talking about pizza for days, a conversation that started with the quote “the end of the Camino is like the last piece of pizza”. So the three of us sought out a restaurant and shared the last pieces of pizza together as a physical representation of our last full day together.

My Italian brother was on a stricter timeline than the rest of us due to his plane ticket. So when he said he wanted to get his Camino-finish tattoo, I decided to go with him. What he got was extremely symbolic. On the first day of the Camino, before I met him, he sped past me with his trekking poles on his shoulders and a Spider-Man hat clipped to his pack. I thought it was hilarious, so I took a picture. That’s the picture he got tattooed on himself. It not only showcased the achievement of his walk, but the bond between us that blossomed over the course of a month.

We regrouped with a group of pilgrims for a night on the town and my birthday quickly became the theme of the night. One of my friends disappeared from the bar we were in just to return from the cold outside 45 minutes later with the legendary cake of the Camino, a Tarta de Santiago. I pulled out the candle from breakfast, had someone light it, and sat there basking in the love as the group sang happy birthday to me in Spanish, English, Portuguese, and Italian, all at the same time. That moment was a memory that would live with me forever.

The rest of the night was full of celebration.

Dinner at a seafood restaurant.

Darts at the legendary pilgrim bar, Pub Momo.

An underground bar with traditional Galician dancing and a jam session from the locals.

And at 3:45 am, I finally lay down; the brothers and I stopped laughing, closing off the day of a beautiful birthday.

Recent findings suggest that marley "Chill Out" Kreiser is continuing her 2026 pilgrimage of the soul on the Camino de Santiago Frances. She fell in love with long walks in nature during her Appalachian Trail 2022 thruhike where she dove into finding herself through the space that the trail provided. Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. This walk is another step into the unknown to embark on "A Saunter of Spirit" as she raises awareness for mental health through raising money for Hike For Mental Health. Donate: https://ihike.org/marleys-camino-hike-for-mental-health/.

Happy (by now belated) Birthday! I have enjoyed sharing your Camino through your posts. The honesty and vulnerability you have been willing to share have inspired me in my own life. It’s clear that your future will take you amazing places both physically and spiritually. Thank you!!

#114517. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • In a recent development, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

In a recent development, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

Recent findings suggest that A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

Recent findings suggest that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

Recent findings suggest that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police said the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Recent findings suggest that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident demonstrates that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

In a recent development, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

Industry observers note that the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the big powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

Sources indicate that after a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) reveals low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

According to recent reports, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps reveals remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Recent findings suggest that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police revealed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

In a recent development, his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#114509. Wildfires Closed 189 Miles of the Pacific Crest Trail in 2026: What 2027 Hikers Need To Know

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (684 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Wildfires Closed 189 Miles of the Pacific Crest Trail in 2026: What 2027 Hikers Need To Know

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to the end-of-year wildfire recap from the Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA), seven fires closed 189 miles of the trail in 2026, burning directly across six miles of the trail itself.
  • California experienced a below-average fire year, while Oregon suffered a record-setting fire year.
  • In Oregon, over 2 million acres burned, but only 6.1 miles of trail were closed from the Badger Butte and Lemiti fires in Mount Hood National Forest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to the end-of-year wildfire recap from the Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA), seven fires closed 189 miles of the trail in 2026, burning directly across six miles of the trail itself.

California experienced a below-average fire year, while Oregon suffered a record-setting fire year. However, the fires in Oregon largely avoided the PCT corridor. In California, 329,000 acres burned, with the PCT seeing brief closures from the Corral and Talbot fires totaling 32.5 miles of trail.

In Oregon, over 2 million acres burned, but only 6.1 miles of trail were closed from the Badger Butte and Lemiti fires in Mount Hood National Forest.

The Badger Butte Fire in Oregon. Photo via PCTA.

Washington, in contrast, experienced the brunt of this year’s closures, especially later into the summer. Trail crews are still working to evaluate the extent of the damage along the trail.

Statewide, over 650,000 acres burned, leading to 150 miles of closed trail from the Ptarmigan, Miners, Three Queens, King, and Sisi fires. Most importantly, the Ptarmigan Fire led to the closure of the northernmost 50 miles of trail, including the Northern Terminus.

Fire has occurred across landscapes along the PCT for thousands of years, often burning at low intensity every few years to a few decades. While low-intensity burns clear brush, replenish soil nutrients, and support new growth, burned trail corridors take years to recover.

Impacts from the older Dixie and Bear fires continue to drop dead timber and sprout heavy brush each year. Across 2025 and 2026, PCTA staff and volunteers cut 3,100 fallen logs in the Bear Fire scar alone, part of more than 23,000 downed trees cleared across the entire PCT since 2024.

Anyone mapping out a 2027 hike on the PCT should prepare for hazards that last well beyond the timeline of an active fire. Closure orders sometimes extend through winter and into the next season, so hikers need to check the PCTA closures page when making plans. Inside these scars, burned timber can topple without warning, especially from wind, making it unsafe to camp or take long breaks under dead trees.

Burned timber is prone to toppling. Photo via Katie Jackson.

Winter weather can also reshape recent burn scars before summer arrives. Scorched slopes are unstable, making them much more prone to landslides. Heavy winter rains could still wash out additional sections before the start of the 2027 hiking season.

Hikers should expect downed trees, overgrown brush, and missing or rough tread. Lost forest canopy also brings more sun exposure and can change water sources, so carrying extra water and checking updated water reports will still be very crucial.

Even with the ill-timed, unfortunately placed closures, a whole group of 2026 hikers still put together rewarding seasons by staying flexible, taking detours, or planning return trips for the missing miles.

“We got off trail at Snoqualmie in August due to the fires. Our only free weekend in October had snow in the forecast, but we went for it! Feeling incredibly lucky to get to the border this year. 2426 miles, what a journey!”  Photo and quote via Brisket & Lamb.

Bringing that same adaptability to the Pacific Crest Trail in 2027 will make navigating the post-fire terrain much easier.

It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (611 w)

Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the newly introduced route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • Expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the newly introduced route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

In a recent development, along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist claims the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

In a recent development, the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

That night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast confirmed a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

Industry observers note that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

It has been revealed that the sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

#114502. Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (469 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • It has been revealed that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

It has been revealed that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

It took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

Sources indicate that at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

According to recent reports, A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

In a recent development, yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Recent findings suggest that tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold new routes here.

According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

Tech Report: Weekend Warm-Up: Hurricane Chase

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (466 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.
  • Sources indicate that the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective.
  • “That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

Sources indicate that the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

Driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

With hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better organization but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Industry observers note that timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

In a recent development, gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the upcoming windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

It’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

#114492. Chasing the Camino Coast

Chasing the Camino Coast

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With nearly 14 miles to hike today, we started early at 6:30 AM.
  • It has been revealed that because Vigo is such a massive port city, our morning walk began right along the waterfront.
  • In a recent development, standing guard near the loading zone was a man carrying a live falcon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With nearly 14 miles to hike today, we started early at 6:30 AM.

It has been revealed that because Vigo is such a massive port city, our morning walk began right along the waterfront. We passed a mile-long fish distribution facility where workers offloaded fresh seafood from ships into warehouses before loading it onto smaller delivery vans.

In a recent development, standing guard near the loading zone was a man carrying a live falcon. He explained that his job is to scare away seagulls that constantly try to swoop in and steal the fish.

Sources indicate that from here, we officially transitioned onto a mix of the Coastal Camino and the parallel Senda Litoral (Litoral Route). While both follow the ocean, the Litoral Route hugs the shoreline much more closely—even winding all the way out around various peninsulas.

In a recent development, after two miles of walking beside roaring city traffic, the trail finally turned into a quiet, intimate medieval village. We took advantage of the peaceful atmosphere and stopped at a local café for pastries and caffeine.

Leaving the café, we wound through narrow village streets and stepped onto a coastal boardwalk stretching over a marshy area beside the bay. We were officially on the Litoral Route now. Because Vigo is a popular starting point for pilgrims walking the minimum 100 km needed to earn their Compostela certificate, we expected to see far fewer crowds on this quieter coastal stretch.

Industry observers note that however, the trail wasn’t very well marked, so we had to rely heavily on digital maps to stay on track. Continuing along the waterfront, we passed through a long, tree-lined park dotted with beachfront bars and nightclubs overlooking the sand—an area that must come alive after dark. Even early in the morning, green parakeets were already out grazing in the grass.

Recent findings suggest that the Camino continued right along the water. A cool breeze blew off the ocean, though the bright sun kept us warm as we passed steep, rocky cliffs broken up by small pockets of sandy beaches. By 11:00 AM, we had already covered 9 miles.

We continued bouncing back and forth between the Coastal and Litoral paths. Eventually, the route ran alongside a busy road at the end of a large bay before leading us down a beachside road past an expansive stretch of sand. Crossing over a river, we finally arrived in the village of A Ramallosa, where our albergue was waiting.

According to recent reports, our accommodations for the night were in a family-run apartment building—the family lived on the top two floors and rented out the bottom two. Conveniently, it sat right behind a beachfront bar where we grabbed dinner. We sat outside enjoying the ocean views and a few drinks until the evening chill pushed us indoors, where we exhaustedly turned in for a great night’s sleep.

American Climber Dies at 5,800m After Summiting Mera Peak

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.
  • According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.
  • Past Mera Peak climbers have suggested on social media that it was unusual to overnight in the high camp after summiting so early in the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.

According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.

He was found dead the next morning. Past Mera Peak climbers have suggested on social media that it was unusual to overnight in the high camp after summiting so early in the day.

His body was evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu for an autopsy. The cause of death remains undetermined. An initial report raised the possibility of altitude-related illness or a cardiac event, but neither has been established medically.

In a recent development, skidmore previously summited Lobuche Peak in 2024, according to the Everest Chronicle and the Italian Alpine Club’s publication Lo Scarpone. So he had previous Himalayan climbing experience above 6,000m.

The Himalayan Database does include Mera Peak, but its coverage of popular trekking peaks is selective. However, it notes that since 2018, four people have died on Mera Peak, not counting Skidmore.

#114486. Road Walking, Fine Dining, and Day Drinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1400 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Road Walking, Fine Dining, and Day Drinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For about 80 miles near its halfway point, the Ice Age Trail is split in two.
  • At Karner Meadow, not far south of the Pleasant Lake bifurcation, I pitched my tent just in time to shelter from a thunderstorm.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Baraboo Hills contain the four biggest climbs on the IAT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For about 80 miles near its halfway point, the Ice Age Trail is split in two. When planning my hike, I decided to go east. It’s five miles longer than the west branch, but has 12 more miles of trail and better overnight options.

At Karner Meadow, not far south of the Pleasant Lake bifurcation, I pitched my tent just in time to shelter from a thunderstorm. It was my first of five nights on the east branch.

Recent findings suggest that the Baraboo Hills contain the four biggest climbs on the IAT. I started my day with number one: almost 700 feet of elevation gain. (Numbers two and four were next. I’d conquered number three the previous afternoon without realizing.) At some point during the uphill, I crossed the boundary into Devil’s Lake State Park, but it was still early, and the trail was empty.

At the first campground, there were few signs of life. I stopped at the small store for a drink and a snack, and in that time, Wisconsin woke up. At the next campground, there were cars and pedestrians everywhere. On the north shore of the lake, there were plenty of people swimming and soaking up the mid-morning sun. (The east and west branches rejoin nearby, fyi.).

Industry observers note that things quietened down during the hike up the West Bluff, and I didn’t meet anyone on the summit ridgeline. For almost a mile, the views were among the best of the entire IAT.

Devil’s Lake, from the West Bluff.

Recent findings suggest that back down at the lake, I found the south shore even busier than the north. I ate an early lunch at the concession stand, then took an extended break before I tackled the East Bluff. The views at the top were also spectacular, and lots of people were enjoying them.

The throngs thinned for a mile or so, and disappeared completely after another mile. I completed my final descent of the day, headed for the Merrimac Ferry, and arrived just in time to see it leave. Still, that gave me time to buy an ice cream. The ferry returned less than 10 minutes later, pulling itself across Lake Wisconsin using three underwater cables.

Sources indicate that the half-mile ferry ride only took a few minutes, but it was enough time for my first ice cream to settle. I bought another ice cream on the south shore, replenished my water supply, and walked one more mile to my campsite. A 2700 foot day might not be huge, but it was my biggest on the IAT. It was also my favorite.

The morning marked the beginning of another three day town-to-town relay. I started by admiring the view from Gibraltar Rock, then made a beeline for Lodi. Piggly Wiggly was my first stop, followed by Dollar General. As I continued south along Main Street, I grabbed the opportunity for a spontaneous game of charades with a nearby motorist.

It has been revealed that A Mazda CX5 was pulling out of a parking lot, and I made what I thought was the universal sign for “Roll your window down.” In fairness to the driver, she was on her own, and car windows haven’t been cranked by hand since before the turn of the century. She shook her head. Undeterred, I strung together a sequence of three more signs. She shook her head again and drove away. In fairness to me, “Your passenger-side rear tire is underinflated” is a difficult message to get across without words. I hope she had second thoughts before starting the drive back to Texas.

I repacked my food on a picnic table in the park, visited a Kwik Trip on my way out of town, and reached my campsite by late afternoon.

Leaving camp, early the next morning.

My next destination was Cross Plains. It was a low mileage day, and I arrived in time for a late lunch: sandwich and Cheetos for my main course, apple fritter and Snickers ice cream for dessert. Afterwards, I visited the IAT Alliance’s office to say hello, then the pavilion beside the library to charge my phone. The afternoon was warm, so I waited in the shade before eventually hiking up a small hill to a dispersed camping area (DCA).

I stopped at the local Kwik Trip again for breakfast. Afterwards, the trail led me through a park, along the edge of some cornfields, and on to quiet country roads. There were lots of speedy Saturday cyclists enjoying the cool, overcast weather.

The rain, when it inevitably began to fall, wasn’t worthy of a rain jacket. I continued following the road along the perimeter of a sprawling residential area until the yellow blazes directed me to cut through the neighborhood. For the next few miles, I squeezed and sidled and slunk between houses and back yards and construction sites. I peered furtively out from between hedges and trees before darting across roads. Similar behavior, I imagined, to foxes and raccoons. I crossed a golf course, passed a handful of soccer fields, and entered Badger Prairie County Park without a moment to spare. Drizzle became downpour, and a park pavilion once again saved me from a soaking. I’d made it to Verona.

According to recent reports, the rain stopped an hour later. I spent another hour in a nearby Culver’s, bought snacks and dinner at Festival Foods, then returned to the park. I waited for the last visitors to leave before putting up my tent at the DCA, in the dark.

I got up at first light, broke camp swiftly, and walked 200 feet to the pavilion. The sun wasn’t fully over the horizon when the first visitor arrived. I charged my phone while eating breakfast, then made use of the drinking fountain and toilet facilities. It was, without a doubt, the most luxurious DCA of the entire trail. Writing a couple of emails delayed me by 40 minutes, and by the time I left, more people had arrived by car and on foot.

Recent findings suggest that there were plenty of hikers enjoying Verona’s extensive trail system as I headed south, but I soon had to return to the road. I also had to make a quick trip to Kwik Trip before leaving town.

Industry observers note that during the next few miles, I left noisy county highway for quiet country road. Eventually, I picked up the trail again. Where the IAT joins the Badger State Trail, I met a friendly cyclist who gave me a recommendation: Dot’s Tavern. An hour later, passing the tiny community of Basco, I made the necessary detour. I was eight miles from where I intended to camp, and it was still morning, so I figured I could spare an hour for a beer and some socializing.

Dot’s is a tiny place, 100 yards from the trail, and was busy that particular Sunday. About 20 people were sitting around a small bar and a handful of tables in what looked like someone’s back yard.

Well, long story short: one hour turned into five, one beer turned into six, and yet again, I ended up racing to a campsite while trying to outrun a thunderstorm. Thank you, Dave, Paul, and Laura, for your conversation. The best days sometimes contain the fewest miles.

Cornfield south of Cross Plains, Wisconsin.

Industry News: Latest Route on Classic Tien Shan Peak

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three Polish climbers have established a newly introduced line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.
  • Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their new 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains.
  • Recent findings suggest that they named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three Polish climbers have established a newly introduced line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.

Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their new 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains. They then spent a further 11 hours returning to base camp.

Recent findings suggest that they named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976. Their line shares the first 250–300m with Barber’s, Makowski told ExplorersWeb.

“According to the information I have, [the remaining 600-650m] was previously unclimbed and had never been attempted by another team,” said Makowski. “We reached the summit ridge and then began rappelling down from there.

Recent findings suggest that corona Hut, the team’s base camp. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

Free Korea Peak — Pik Svobodnaya Koreya in Russian — was already famous among mountaineers in the former Soviet Union because of its 900m north wall. in 2018, Russian climber Valery Balesin suggested that it was no longer possible to find fresh lines on this well-known face, although advances in steep ice-climbing techniques have clearly opened new possibilities.

“My friends and I researched Free Korea Peak and realized that part of the north face still has unclimbed terrain,” said Makowski.

It has been revealed that on the Polish Barber route. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

It has been revealed that their route was almost completely ice climbing. The crux came midway up the wall, when they faced a particularly steep section of ice that they graded at Alpine Ice 4+. The rest of the route was 3/3+. Fortunately, “protection on the Polish Barber was really good, except for the last 150m, where ice was pretty thin and crusty,” said Makowski.

According to recent reports, climbing by moonlight. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

Sources indicate that despite its former popularity, they had the valley almost to themselves during their week in camp. There was just one Russian group doing a tourist trek up nearby Corona Peak.

Ukrainian Solos Fresh Route in Gokyo Valley, Near Everest

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (306 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a upcoming route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m).
  • Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive fresh route.
  • According to recent reports, the Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a upcoming route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m). Also known as Machhermo Peak, it sits 24km west of Everest in the Gokyo Valley.

Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive fresh route.

According to recent reports, the Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19. He made two bivouacs on the way up and one more on the descent.

“The level of difficulty is hard to tell, as always when solo, but I’d say it was around 80° on ice, M5+, 5c on rock, and lots of poor snow!” Balavanov said.

He estimates the new route is 1,200m long, and spans some 850 vertical meters from base to summit.

According to recent reports, rough topo of Balabanov’s solo route on the northeast face of Phari Lapcha. Photo: Mykyta Balabanov.

Sources indicate that another side of Phari Lapcha saw action just one day before Balabanov, when U.S. guide Bennie Lieber led Canadian Emma Deguara up the Stone(d) Yeti route on the south face.

“I was not related to that climb, as I climbed alone after approaching from a different valley,” Balabanov explained. “However, I saw their tracks on the summit and spotted their bivy place at the bottom of the south face.”.

Lieber and Deguara made the second ascent of their chosen route. “While the technical grade (M3, AI2+) is easily digestible, the room for mistakes, due to exposure, is zero,” Lieber said.

Mykyta Balabanov and fellow Ukrainian Mikhail Fomino opened a upcoming route on Ama Dablam in 2024, but they first became widely known for their new route on the Southeast Ridge of Annapurna III in 2021.
